When we discussed pre-Islamic proverbs, we noted that they preserve some of the knowledge Arabs had at the time about nature and thought.
In reality, they accumulated this knowledge through direct experience.
But it was naturally scattered and unorganized because it arose from ordinary daily experience rather than from deliberate investigation aimed at gaining knowledge for its own sake.
People learned these things while responding to immediate and recurring practical needs in the normal course of life.
Once acquired, some of this knowledge could serve as a basis for analogy. People began to treat what they had learned as standards or general rules that could be applied to similar situations.
But this still did not amount to what we today call scientific knowledge.
Pre-Islamic knowledge lacked systematic induction, the organized drawing of conclusions, and the linking of separate results into a coherent scientific system.
This limitation was completely natural in its historical setting.
But it does not mean that the basic elements needed for the growth of a distinct pre-Islamic culture were absent.
For this reason, we think Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq was right when he wrote:

“Whatever the condition of the Arabs at the appearance of the Muhammadan religion, intellectually they were not at the level of the earliest and most simple human communities, at least in the area that concerns us here”—meaning the beginnings of philosophical thought—“as can be seen from what we know of their religions and what has been transmitted of their literary remains.”

“Whatever may be true, imaginary, or exaggerated in the reports about the sages and judges of the pre-Islamic Arabs, these reports still tell us something about the kind of thinking that the Arabs called wisdom and about the people whom they called sages and judges.
“It was practical thought, connected with deciding disputes that arose among them, giving judgments on problems they faced, and treating illnesses that affected them...”
There was indeed a group among the Arabs whose level of culture was somewhat higher than that of the population around them.

These were the sages. Alongside the knowledge gained from experience, they preserved many sound proverbs and memorable sayings that circulated among followers of the different religions that had contact with the Arabian Peninsula in more than one region.
Early Arab historians also wrote about the knowledge of the pre-Islamic Arabs.
Ṣāʿid al-Andalusī, writing in the eleventh century, said that they possessed knowledge:

“of the times when the stars rise and set, and of the stellar signs and the rains associated with them. They acquired this through close attention and long experience because they needed such knowledge for their livelihood, not because they were trying to learn the underlying truths or train themselves in the sciences.”
This final point in Ṣāʿid’s statement reflects a sound historical method.
He explains pre-Islamic knowledge as the result of spontaneous experience arising from practical needs, not from a conscious attempt to pursue knowledge for its own sake.
That matches what we said earlier.
Ibn Khaldūn offers a similar explanation.

He argues that the Arabs in their early period, around the rise of Islam, did not possess the sciences that later flourished under Islamic rule because their society was still simple and largely Bedouin, and because teaching, authorship, and the systematic recording of knowledge had not yet developed among them.
It is clear that Ibn Khaldūn does not explain the absence of organized scientific knowledge among the early Arabs by appealing to some permanent Arab racial nature.
He explains it through the conditions of their life at that particular stage of history.
In this respect, Ibn Khaldūn is using a scientific method of research.
We now come to the way pre-Islamic Arabs approached questions of knowledge.
Did their thinking contain any genuine rational reflection?
Or did they simply accumulate information from everyday experience in response to the practical needs of daily life?
The first thing that draws our attention is that the words “wisdom” and “sages” were widely used in pre-Islamic Arabia.

The word “wisdom” was used for a particular kind of speech found in the work of poets such as Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā, especially in his famous Muʿallaqa, and in the speeches of people such as Quss ibn Sāʿida al-Iyādī and the soothsayers.
The term was also applied to the behavior and judgments of people who were known at the time as “sages.”
Among them were al-Ḥārith ibn Kalada al-Thaqafī and his son al-Naḍr ibn al-Ḥārith.
People turned to such figures when immediate problems arose in their lives.

They acted much like judges in settling disputes. They applied rules handed down through social custom to new situations. They also advised individuals and guided them toward what they regarded as good social behavior.
Aḥmad Amīn believed that the Arab “sages” represented the most intellectually advanced group among them.
If we then look at how the meanings of “wisdom” and “sage” developed after Islam, and especially after the rise of philosophy, we find something suggestive.
“Wisdom” eventually came to mean philosophy itself, while “sage” came to mean philosopher.
This gives us some reason to think that even in the pre-Islamic period, these words referred to an early and simple form of rational reflection.
It was still spontaneous and unsystematic, but it attempted to draw general judgments from individual cases and then apply those judgments to later situations by analogy.
This kind of thinking already involves the use of reason.
It takes something general from particular cases through a basic act of abstraction. Then it brings that general rule back to a new particular case and applies it there.
That too is a form of rational reflection.
Pre-Islamic thought, however, did not yet carry out this process with a conscious understanding of the separate steps involved.

If we return here to the dialectical relationship between language and human life, we can once again draw a clear conclusion. The words “wisdom” and “sages,” in the developed sense discussed above, could not have existed in the language of the pre-Islamic Arabs—or been used as they were—unless those Arabs had actually possessed some degree of what we have called rational thought.

Of course, we do not mean that this kind of rational thinking had developed beyond what the historical conditions of their society could support. Nor do we mean that rational thought in the pre-Islamic period had already reached the level of philosophy.
One example of this early form of rational thinking may be found in the following observation:

“The Arabs’ long experience of herding livestock drew them away from medicine based on divination and superstition and brought them closer to medicine based on practical experience. They observed pregnancy, birth, growth, and the various biological stages connected with them. They dissected bodies and gained some knowledge of the location of the organs and the functions those organs performed in the animal body. As a result, they came reasonably close to explaining the causes of illness and recovery.”

What interests us here is the final point: their attempt to explain illness and recovery. This is in itself an act of reasoning. It uses the results of direct sensory experience to draw broader conclusions.

Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq noticed something even clearer and more specific. He wrote that, at the time Islam appeared, the Arabs were already engaging in “forms of rational inquiry that came close to philosophical investigation, since they dealt with questions beyond the physical world: the nature of God, whether the world was eternal or created, souls, angels, jinn, and similar matters.” He also says that when the Qur’an was being revealed, the Arabs were already “arguing and debating religious beliefs,” and that questions such as the sending of prophets, life after death, and the resurrection of the dead were especially disputed among the different religious groups.
Al-Maqrīzī, Taqī al-Dīn Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī (d. 845 AH/1441 CE), also makes a revealing observation on this subject. He writes:

“The name ‘philosophers’ is applied to certain groups in India, including the naturalists and the Brahmins. They practice severe forms of spiritual discipline and deny prophecy altogether. The name is also applied to the Arabs, though in a lesser sense. Their wisdom comes from their own reflections and from observing nature. They accept prophecy, but they are weaker in the sciences. Among the philosophers are also the sages of the Greeks, who fall into several groups: the early pillars of wisdom, the Peripatetics, the Stoics, the followers of Aristotle, and the philosophers of Islam.”

By “the Arabs, though in a lesser sense,” al-Maqrīzī means the Arabs before Islam. Two things make this clear. First, he says that “their wisdom comes from their own reflections and from observing nature,” a description that fits the pre-Islamic Arabs. Second, he separately mentions “the philosophers of Islam” at the end of the passage. So the word “Arabs” in the earlier sentence clearly does not include philosophers of the Islamic period.

Al-Maqrīzī therefore believed that the Arabs before Islam had their own “philosophers,” though in his view they deserved the name less fully than others. He also gave a sound and realistic explanation for why this was so.

We would not, of course, go as far as al-Maqrīzī and call the pre-Islamic Arabs “philosophers.” But his comments do support the conclusion that some degree of rational inquiry existed among them. What he called “philosophy” is what interests us here.
F — Religious Phenomena in Pre-Islamic Society
Before discussing the religious phenomena of the pre-Islamic period, we need to establish an important fact.

Religion, whatever form its beliefs and teachings take in different periods, does not suddenly appear among people in isolation from their earthly lives. It is not cut off from the historical development of their society, economy, politics, or ideas. Nor does religion arise simply because individuals want it to.

Hegel made this point in his Lectures on the History of Philosophy when discussing the relationship between religion and philosophy. He was responding to those who claimed that religion arose from tyranny and anger, or from priests who deliberately deceived the people for selfish purposes.
Hegel was right to reject this view. Religion cannot be explained as the product of a private desire on the part of one group of people, whether priests or anyone else.

Religion has its own social roots. It also has roots in the development of human knowledge. The history of human thought and the history of religion show that religious belief and human knowledge have always influenced one another.
For forces that oppose progress, however, it is very important to present religion as something separate from its social roots, and especially as something completely detached from class struggle.

Within this same ideological outlook, many historians of Islam, both old and modern, have worked hard to present Islam, first, as the beginning of a completely new history for the Arabs, entirely disconnected from their life before Islam. In this view, everything Islam brought—its teachings, beliefs, concepts, and laws—had no connection at all with the Arabs’ earlier past, whether recent or remote.

Second, these historians have tried to make the history of Arab thought begin with the rise of Islam, as though the Arabs had possessed no earlier intellectual or cultural heritage worth mentioning. Islam is made to look as though it created the Arabs from nothing.

This view of Islam, and of Arab history before Islam, is wrong in three ways. First, it contradicts historical reality. Second, it is opposed to scientific knowledge. Third, it conflicts with Islam’s own texts, teachings, and laws.

It contradicts reality because a large body of historically and scientifically reliable evidence shows that Arab history before and after Islam forms one continuous history. Everything that appeared openly or beneath the surface of Arab society after the rise of Islam was part of the further development of conditions that already existed during the pre-Islamic period, especially in its final stage during the sixth and early seventh centuries.

This view is also opposed to science because everything we know from the study of social and cultural development rules out the idea that religion can suddenly appear in a society, at a particular moment, from outside that society’s history and outside the wider course of human development.

Social science, when it studies the objective and dialectical patterns of human history, shows that every religion arose as an incomplete reflection, in people’s ideas and beliefs, of the social relationships that existed at a particular stage of history.

It is therefore wrong to explain the appearance of any religion as an event cut off from the concrete course of human life on earth. No religion in human history has appeared at a level beyond the concrete social relations of the society in which it arose.

So we return to our earlier point: every religion that has appeared in history has had social roots in the part of the world where it emerged. It has also had roots in the development of human knowledge and experience.

Finally, the view of Islam described above also conflicts with Islam’s own texts and teachings. Those texts preserve many features of pre-Islamic Arab history, customs, traditions, and laws. Islam kept some of them, changed others, and rejected those that could no longer survive alongside the new social relations already beginning to emerge within pre-Islamic society itself, as we explained earlier in this chapter.
Of all the religious phenomena found in Arab society shortly before the rise of Islam, paganism was the most widespread and had the deepest historical roots.
As the earliest form of religion in human history, and as the most basic expression of religious belief, paganism can be traced far back into Arab history.

We still lack scientifically accepted evidence that would allow us to date its beginnings precisely. But we can go back at least to the period of the Sabaean state in Yemen, which dates to around the eighth century BCE.

Modern excavations uncovered the remains of a theatre connected to a large temple, together with an impressive set of terraces. Archaeologists were able to identify this great structure as the “Temple of the Sun” and to establish that it belonged to the Sabaean state. This means that the people of Yemen under that state worshipped the sun.
Paganism continued after that in different forms throughout the Arabian Peninsula, down to the sixth century and the period immediately before Islam.

At some point, however, the historical development of the people of the peninsula suffered a break for reasons that remain unclear. Historians mention among the possible causes the collapse of the Maʾrib Dam in Yemen, which had been built by the Ḥimyarite state. Its collapse caused a great flood that drowned farmland, displaced the population, and forced many people to migrate beyond the peninsula to Syria, Palestine, and elsewhere. This is the flood known as the “Flood of al-ʿArim,” which is also mentioned in the Qur’an, as the historical accounts tell us.
This break in history interrupted the earlier course of development in the peninsula.

As a result, from the first centuries CE until the sixth century, we see a kind of cultural regression. The development achieved under the Sabaean, Minaean, and Ḥimyarite states did not continue along the same upward path. A primitive communal system and a largely nomadic way of life came to dominate, until the later pre-Islamic period, when the first signs of class division began to appear.
This helps explain why very early forms of pagan religion were still present so late in Arab history—for example, the placing of idols in the Kaaba as symbols of gods and objects of worship.
We have already seen that idol worship around the Kaaba eventually acquired a class character. The Quraysh leadership used it as a means of maintaining control, exploiting others, and making profits.

Alongside these forms of paganism, however, there were others resembling the religions of the more developed ancient Arabs of Yemen. As we have seen, these included the worship of heavenly bodies such as the sun, moon, and Venus, as well as other cosmic and natural phenomena.
There was also some fire worship among certain tribes. This may have reached them through contact with the Zoroastrians of Persia, given their geographical proximity and commercial relations.

The Qur’an also refers to tendencies within pre-Islamic pagan belief that departed from the dominant religious outlook. One of these is the tendency Islamic writers call the Dahriyya. The Qur’anic passages suggest that these people either denied creation and a Creator, denied only life after death, or denied prophecy alone.
In pre-Islamic usage, dahr means time. Their use of this term, together with other expressions carrying a similar meaning, seems to have reflected their belief in fate.
Although paganism was the most visible form of religion in the Arabian Peninsula during the sixth century, Judaism and Christianity also had a strong presence in some areas.
It appears that both religions first entered among tribes living in the northwestern regions bordering Syria and Palestine, where Arab populations also lived.

The first major centre of Judaism inside the peninsula was Yathrib and the surrounding areas of the Hijaz. From there it spread into Yemen, where it became so firmly established that by the beginning of the sixth century it had become the religion of the state.
Judaism then played a visible role in the conflict between the Ḥimyarites and the Abyssinians.

Most historians describe this conflict as though it were purely religious—a struggle between Judaism and Christianity. But although it took a religious form, it was in essence a political conflict between the rulers of Abyssinia and the Ḥimyarites.

After the sea route across the Indian Ocean between India and Africa had been discovered, the Ḥimyarites began using it for maritime trade from some time after the first century CE. This trade grew under their control, and they eventually built towns along the Red Sea coast in response to its expansion.
These Yemeni coastal towns became transit points for valuable goods bound for Byzantium.
At the same time, Byzantine influence was spreading in Abyssinia alongside Christianity. The Byzantines began to seek control of Yemen’s strategic commercial position.

As so often happens when religion is used in the service of political ambition, the Abyssinians began attacking Ḥimyarite positions in Yemen in the name of Christianity, while in reality serving Byzantine political aims. Religion was also used to win the Christians of Yemen over as allies of Abyssinia.

The Ḥimyarites responded by encouraging the spread of Judaism in their own country. Judaism therefore also became a political weapon, used against Christianity because Christianity had become an instrument of Abyssinian policy.
